THOUGHT: The patient is a woman in her 60s with a remote history of left breast carcinoma and prior regional metastasis. She presents with a subacute (3-month) unilateral violaceous, telangiectatic, edematous eruption of the face with necrosis. Biopsy shows dilated dermal vessels containing nests of highly atypical cells. Immunohistochemistry demonstrates that the atypical cells are strongly GATA3-positive (a sensitive marker for breast (and urothelial) epithelial origin), while endothelial cells are CD31-positive. The morphology—tumor cell nests within vascular/lymphovascular spaces in the dermis—plus the strong GATA3 staining is most consistent with cutaneous metastasis of breast carcinoma manifesting as intravascular tumor emboli/carcinoma erysipeloides or the telangiectatic metastatic pattern. Other entities that can produce violaceous telangiectatic plaques and show CD31 positivity (angiosarcoma, Kaposi sarcoma) are considered but are less likely because their neoplastic cells are endothelial (not GATA3-positive epithelial tumor cells) and histology differs (malignant vascular channels or spindle-cell proliferation rather than intravascular epithelial nests). Intravascular lymphoma can occlude dermal vessels but would express lymphoid markers, not GATA3. Infectious/inflammatory cellulitis or erysipelas is clinically possible but is inconsistent with biopsy showing malignant epithelial cells.

DIAGNOSIS:
1. Cutaneous metastatic breast carcinoma with intravascular tumor emboli (carcinoma erysipeloides / telangiectatic cutaneous metastasis) — most likely given history and strong GATA3 positivity in atypical cells.
2. Cutaneous angiosarcoma (including radiation-associated angiosarcoma) — clinically similar and CD31+ endothelium, but less likely because malignant cells would be endothelial (GATA3−) and histology differs.
3. Kaposi sarcoma — can produce violaceous telangiectatic plaques and is CD31+, but histology (HHV‑8+ spindle cell proliferation) and lack of GATA3 make this less likely.
4. Primary cutaneous intravascular large cell lymphoma — can present with violaceous patches from vascular occlusion, but would show lymphoid markers (CD20/CD3) rather than epithelial GATA3 positivity.
5. Infectious/inflammatory cellulitis or erysipelas (chronic/atypical presentation) or radiation dermatitis mimicking erythema — clinically possible but unlikely given biopsy-proven malignant epithelial cells.

A woman in her 60s presented with a 3-month history of pain, swelling, and erythema on her face. Medical history includes left breast carcinoma diagnosed eleven years earlier, treated with mastectomy, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy. Seven years after initial diagnosis, she had left supraclavicular lymph nodes metastasis treated with surgical excision. Current symptoms include pain on palpation, with no fever or chills.

Physical Examination:
Violaceous swelling with telangiectasia and necrosis on the forehead, eyelids, nose, and cheek, predominantly involving the left side of the face.

Diagnostic Tests:
- Histopathological examination:  Findings: Hyperkeratosis, epidermal atrophy, and dilated vessels in the dermis. One vessel showed nests of highly atypical cells.    - Immunohistochemical examination:  Results: Epithelial cells in the dilated vessels were positive for CD31, and the atypical cells were strongly positive for GATA3.    - Images:  Figure 1 Title: Full and three-quarters image of the face  Figure 1 Description: Telangiectatic, swelling erythema mainly involving the left side of the forehead, eyelids, nose, and cheek    Figure 2 Title: Histopathological and immunohistochemical images  Figure 2A Description: Highly atypical cells in a dilated vessel in the dermis (hematoxylin-eosin stain; original magnification, ×10)  Figure 2B Description: Atypical cells in dilated vessels (streptavidin-peroxidase stain; original magnification, ×20)
